title: Apple Is Facing 2 Big Tests Right Now -- Here's a Common-Sense Solution
text:
Apple Is Facing 2 Big Tests Right Now -- Here's a Common-Sense Solution By aapl
Apple ( AAPL ) is scheduled to report second quarter earnings on May 1. Anticipation is building as analysts are already weighing in with their predictions.
Last week, Apple was rallying and appeared ready to make another run at its all-time closing high of $181.72. Then a Wall Street analyst indicated that iPhone sales would be significantly lower than anticipated in the third quarter.
On Friday, Morgan Stanley analyst Katy Huberty lowered her estimate for iPhone sales for Apple's third quarter to 34 million from 40.5 million. Most analysts have pegged Apple's iPhone sales at 43 million for the quarter. The news came on the heels of similar negative comments from Bank of America and J.P. Morgan analysts earlier in the week.
Clearly, the comments spooked investors, as Apple sold off on heavy volume. Apple's chart is notable because of where the stock temporarily stopped falling, on its 200-day moving average (red). The $165 area is also home to a cluster of support from last month (shaded yellow).
After Tuesday's selloff, the stock has largely traded below its 200-day MA. The break lower opens the door for a potential move to $155, a support area left over from February (shaded blue). If that also breaks, there really isn't much to discuss in terms of nearby technical support.
Source: TradeStation
Morgan Stanley's Huberty insists that any selloff is a buying opportunity, for several reasons. First, Apple Services remains an outstanding growth story. One analyst, Horace Dediu of Asymco, estimates that customers will spend $100 million per day in Apple's app store by the end of this year. Huberty also cites Apple's massive cash pile as a source of downside protection.
How can Action Alerts PLUS holding Apple solve the problem of constantly dealing with changing expectations for iPhone sales and its other products? Apple's Services is successful in part because it generates a steady and increasing stream of capital. Is there a way to do the same for the iPhone?
Since many iPhone sales are upgrades, why not offer the product on a subscription basis? For example, Apple could offer the phone on a three-year and/or five-year subscription plan. Subscribers would always get the newest iteration of the iPhone at a discount as part of the deal.
In fact, Apple could offer a wide variety of subscriptions and deals. Subscribe to the iPhone and iPad and get Apple Music for free. Subscribe to the iPhone, iPad, and iMac and get a free or discounted Apple Watch. The possibilities are endless.
This would solve several problems; it would smooth out the lumpiness in sales and make cycles more predictable. Most important of all, it would pull consumers deeper into the Apple ecosystem, generating additional income for Services.
